#3175. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

#3174. It’s Official: Anthropic Prices Its IPO at $83 a Share. Here’s What We Know (and What We Don’t)

Anthropic’s IPO was priced above its range, and the final raise could rival SpaceX’s record deal.

By Matt Frankel, CFP® – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:17PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

Anthropic, the company behind the Claude family of AI models, priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, according to Reuters, Bloomberg and CNBC, which all cited people familiar with the matter. That's well above the $70-$78 range the company set when it launched its roadshow last week.

Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT. Pricing above the range is a strong sign of demand and sets up one of the largest IPOs on record, as well as the first from a major developer of frontier AI models.

Anthropic originally planned to sell 825 million shares, about 801 million of which would be offered by the company and the remainder from existing shareholders. At $83 apiece, that share count alone would raise about $68.5 billion. Anthropic also lined up a $26 billion private placement with major chip, cloud, and software companies, bringing the combined total to more than $94 billion. And at $83 per share, Anthropic would be valued at approximately $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

SpaceX (SPCX +1.27%) set the IPO record in June, raising $75 billion by selling about 555.6 million shares at $135 each. Including the extra shares sold to underwriters, the total came to about $86.2 billion. At its original share count, Anthropic's IPO would come in slightly below SpaceX's base deal, but it would require only about 10% more shares to match it. With the private placement included, Anthropic's total fundraising would already top what SpaceX raised.

A few important details aren't official yet. Bloomberg and Reuters both reported that Anthropic was likely to upsize the offering (sell more shares than originally planned), but Anthropic hasn't disclosed how many shares it's selling. Until it does, we don't know the final amount raised, whether this becomes the largest IPO ever, or the exact valuation. We also don't know whether the underwriters will buy additional shares or where the stock will open on Thursday. As with many hot IPO stocks, the first trade could come well above $83.

#3173. Jensen Huang says he’s ready to rejoin Nvidia as CEO (if asked)

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

What do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

#3172. Microsoft says Copilot beats Claude and ChatGPT on price

The cost claim rests on a study Microsoft paid for, and Anthropic's own figures look far lower.

Microsoft told its Ignite conference that businesses choose Copilot over Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT because it is cheaper to run, citing a study it commissioned from GigaOm. Anthropic says non-coding Claude Enterprise users spend under $75 a month, well below the study’s $205 figure.

Microsoft says companies are choosing its Copilot AI assistant over Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT because it costs less to run, Bloomberg reported. Judson Althoff, who runs Microsoft’s commercial business, made the pitch at the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday. Microsoft has coached its salespeople to pitch Copilot against both rivals since July.

“Anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot, and for less,” Althoff said.

The claim leans on a study Microsoft paid research firm GigaOm to run, which found users would spend much less on Copilot. That study cited $205 a month per user for basic work. Anthropic says its non-coding Claude Enterprise users spend under $75 a month on average.

AI bills have become a big worry for companies this year, with many capping staff AI use. Copilot offers a flat monthly fee for basic tasks, or pay-as-you-go pricing for heavier work. Microsoft itself cut back Claude Code licences for its own engineers in May over token costs.

Copilot had more than 30 million paid users in June, a small share of the 450 million business users of Microsoft’s office software. Its daily users grew fivefold in a year, Microsoft said last month. AT&T pays for tens of thousands of staff to use it, though it also uses OpenAI’s Codex.

The fight is getting personal. Last week Anthropic added Claude Sheets and other office tools aimed at Excel. Microsoft’s Jacob Andreou said at Ignite that rivals’ “simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration.”

#3169. Understand How Satellite Links Shape IoT Device Design and Testing

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

#3168. VSCO launches its first native Mac photo editor with RAW support, batch editing, more

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, users can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:

#3166. Stock Market Today, Nov. 18: Recursion Pharmaceuticals Rises 4% on FDA Alignment for REC-4881 Phase 3 Design

On Nov. 18, 2026, Recursion shares climbed after regulators aligned on its lead familial adenomatous polyposis trial, though investors are watching for more detail.

By Josh Kohn-Lindquist – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:20PM EST

Recursion Pharmaceuticals (RXRX +3.86%), an AI-enabled clinical-stage drug discovery company, closed at $2.83, up 3.86%. The stock rose after the company said it reached FDA alignment on the REC-4881 Phase 3 design, and investors are watching for further regulatory detail. Trading volume reached 39.4M shares, coming in about 65% above its three-month average of 23.8M shares. Recursion Pharmaceuticals IPO'd in 2021 and has fallen 91% since going public.

S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.23%) closed at 7,323, down 0.24%, while Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +0.42%) finished at 24,430, up 0.42%. In biotechnology: AI-enabled drug discovery and clinical-stage therapeutics, Schrödinger (SDGR +6.00%) closed at $27.20, up 6.00%, and Relay Therapeutics (RLAY +0.24%) closed at $16.51, up 0.24%.

Recursion shares are up 4% today after it aligned with the FDA on a Phase III trial design for 200 adults with familial adenomatous polyposis. The disease currently has no approved therapies, making Recursion's REC-4881 one of the first AI-enabled treatments to advance toward a Phase III trial.

Recursion believes there are over 50,000 patients with familial adenomatous polyposis in the U.S. and E.U., representing a $15 billion market opportunity for the $1.7 billion company. The FDA accepted 10 mm or larger polyp excision as part of its primary endpoint of event-free survival, which could be a win for RXRX stock, as it shouldn't have to run a longer, costlier trial waiting for adverse events to develop further.

While today's development is great progress for the stock, the results of the Phase III trial itself remain paramount, as success with REC-4881 would serve as a proof of concept not just for Recursion but for its AI platform. The Phase III trial won't begin until the second half of 2027, however, so interested investors need to be uber-patient and risk-tolerant before considering this stock.

Downdetector is showing reports across multiple Apple services, even as Apple’s System Status page continues to list them as available.

Affected services include the App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay, Apple Support, iPhone Activation, and more.

Apple confirms a number of services experiencing issues on its general and developer status pages.

Apple retail stores and corporate offices are also reportedly experiencing outages.

Others say the App Store won’t load or download apps, while Apple Music and device activation are also running into problems. Developers have separately reported trouble accessing App Store Connect.

The number of "coincidental" system failure happening these days make it difficult to believe it's not cyberattacks, AI failures, or both. Even more suspicious is that they all seem to be reciting the same script for the cause: "an internal update".

The disruption follows last week’s widespread Microsoft Outlook outage.

Yesterday, banking services also experienced problems after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted online access and delayed some transactions involving other banks.

Are Apple services working for you? Let us know what you’re seeing in the comments.

Update: Apple now says an internal update caused the outage, ruling out a cyber attack, and many services are coming back online. Consumer-facing services are back online. Developer-focused services are still experiencing issues.

Apple: “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible." Company says this wasn’t a cyberattack.

#3163. Google opens its Genie 4 world model to AI Ultra subscribers

Users can now reshape AI-generated worlds as they explore them, and hear them too.

Genie 4 creates a world you can move through, and lets you change it as you go. Typing a prompt mid-session can shift the weather, add a character or redirect what happens. It also adds sound for the first time, from background noise to character dialogue.

Google DeepMind first showed Genie 4 to testers in October. The new release adds an AI agent that builds worlds from a conversation, and a gallery where users can share and remix each other’s worlds. Project Genie already lets some users explore simulated cities built from Street View.

The older Genie 3 stays available for longer runs, and now lasts up to three minutes per generation, up from 60 seconds. Big game studios remain wary, and Take-Two says GTA 6 used no generative AI.

Google says both models are still research systems. Details can drift in long sessions, and readable text and complex physics remain hard. Everything made in Project Genie carries SynthID, Google’s invisible watermark for AI content.

World models are drawing big money: AMD agreed to buy Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs for $8.2B in September. Google DeepMind says such models could also train robots and AI agents before they work in the real world. Rival lab Odyssey says its Odyssey-3 model can already control robots and cars.

The Google Wallet app on iPhone does not offer tap-to-pay functionality due to platform restrictions. Instead, Google touts three intended use cases:

App navigation is handled by a floating pill (in Liquid Glass) with two tabs. The homepage starts with a carousel of recent purchases slated for delivery, followed by boarding passes, and finally a grid of loyalty cards.

#3160. Billionaire Bill Ackman Sold 2 Million Shares of Microsoft Stock. But Here's Why He Says He's Still Bullish

Pershing Square's latest filing shows a big cut in its Microsoft stake, but Ackman says it omits what he bought instead.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:22PM EST

At first glance, Pershing Square's latest quarterly holdings report might suggest that billionaire Bill Ackman soured on Microsoft (MSFT +0.41%) stock. But he says that's the wrong read, and his reasoning makes perfect sense.

The filing shows his firm held 4,064,779 Microsoft shares on Sept. 30, down from 6,206,730 three months earlier. That's a cut of about 2.1 million shares, or roughly a third of the position.

On Wednesday, Ackman explained on X what the filing leaves out. In July, Pershing Square bought 2 million "deep-in-the-money" options on Microsoft, with a strike price of about $310 a share and a term of two and a half years. Those options were bought over the counter, which excludes them from the quarterly filing.

"We remain bullish on Microsoft and believe the stock remains undervalued," he wrote.

Count the options, and Pershing Square's bet on Microsoft is about the same size as before: roughly 4.1 million shares plus options on 2 million more, compared with 6.2 million shares in June.

A deep-in-the-money option behaves much like the underlying stock. With Microsoft at $506.24 at Tuesday's close, an option to buy at $310 rises and falls nearly dollar-for-dollar with the shares. But it costs less up front than buying the stock outright, which frees up cash for other ideas. Ackman said only that the firm occasionally makes the swap "for portfolio management or other reasons."

That said, if Microsoft were to fall below $310 before the options expire, they could end up worthless, a risk that owning the shares doesn't carry.

Microsoft wasn't the only move. Pershing Square opened new positions in Alcon (ALC +1.55%), worth about $954 million, and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE -0.24%), worth about $1 billion. It sold its small remaining stake in Hertz (HTZ -3.70%).

It also trimmed several of its biggest holdings. The firm sold about 11% of its Meta Platforms (META -0.40%) shares, 11% of its Mastercard (MA -0.36%), 12% of its Visa (V -0.37%), 11% of its Brookfield (BN -0.51%) and 15% of its Restaurant Brands International (QSR +0.07%). The one big addition was Netflix (NFLX +0.23%), where it raised its stake by about 18% to 15.4 million shares.

Its largest positions by value at the end of September were Uber Technologies (UBER -0.07%) at $2.35 billion, Amazon (AMZN +3.82%) at $2.12 billion, Microsoft at $2.08 billion and Meta at $2.05 billion.

The lesson is to be careful with 13F filings. They show only the stock and listed options held at the end of each quarter, and they are released weeks later. Private options deals, short positions, and anything bought or sold since then don't appear. Simply comparing filings might yield a headline saying a famous investor "dumped" a stock, when in reality, the conviction hasn't changed.

Ultimately, Ackman's Microsoft bet hasn't really shrunk, and long-term investors can still consider this a vote of confidence from one of Wall Street's best-known stock pickers.

OpenAI kicked off the GPT-6 generation with Astra in September, then upgraded Sol to GPT-6.1 a few weeks later at DevDay.

Today, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are coming to ChatGPT Work and Codex together. OpenAI says both can finish demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done before hitting your usage limit.

Astra is still the model OpenAI recommends for your hardest projects.

Say you have a screenshot of a slide and want the rest of your presentation to look like it. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra can use that screenshot as a template and match the layout, colors, and even the font size.

On the Codex side, OpenAI says Astra is better at making and testing changes in an existing project.

“Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision,” OpenAI says.

Sol is the more affordable model for everyday coding and writing, and it gets surprisingly close to Astra on one coding test.

Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 measures whether changes to real codebases are good enough for maintainers to merge.

With both models at maximum reasoning effort, OpenAI says Sol came within half a point of Astra at about one-fifth the cost.

The iPhone Duo is easily one of Apple’s most ambitious smartphones yet, but its jaw-dropping $1,999 starting price puts it firmly out of reach for most budgets. Foldable phones generally command a premium over conventional slabs, but T-Mobile’s Black Friday promotion lands you a free iPhone Duo for a limited time.

To snag this generous offer, you’ll need to select the “7 Picks” promotion, which gives you up to $2,100 back via 36 monthly bill credits on a qualifying T-Mix plan. The exact steps for getting the iPhone Duo for free are a bit murky, so I’ll walk through everything you need to know.

iPhone Duo: free w/T-Mix plan and "7 picks" promo @ T-MobileThe iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable phone and pairs a 5.4-inch outer screen with an expansive 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR with a nearly invisible crease. You'll be able to watch videos better with the main display, along with true side-by-side multitasking.

In order to get a free iPhone Duo, you need to “unlock” the 7 Picks offer. It all starts with setting up a multi-line account on T-Mobile’s T-Mix More plan (or higher) and committing to it for 36 months. Due to how T-Mix plans allot “Picks” based on your plan tier and line count, a single line won’t cut it — so you definitely need four lines on T-Mix More. This comes out to $180/month with AutoPay.

I selected the base model with 256GB, since the other options incur additional payments. For example, the 2TB option costs $12.50/month for 36 months. Additionally, you need to port in a number to get the free promo — otherwise, a new phone number doesn’t qualify and results in an additional cost.

For the remaining three lines, it gets tricky because you can either bring your own phone or look through T-Mobile’s lineup to see which one best suits your needs. Thankfully, there are several that are “free” — though they’re mostly entry-level models like the Moto G (2026) and Galaxy A17. Whatever you do, I like that you can choose to either port a number or get a new one.

By setting up four lines with this plan, you satisfy the “7 Picks” required for this promo. As a result, you have nothing to pay for the devices at checkout because all four lines come with free phone promotions. Your monthly bill totals $180 per month plus tax, which adds up to $6,480 over 36 months.

While that amount might look shocking, just know you’re getting four lines with unlimited talk, text, and premium data — along with the ability to stream up to 4K UHD video. The best part about this T-Mobile Black Friday deal is that you ultimately pay nothing for the iPhone Duo.

#3157. The CEO behind GTA VI doesn’t play games. Analysts say he bet up to $1.5B

Strauss Zelnick says being a gamer doesn't make a better boss, and his biggest bet launches on Thursday.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick has run the company since 2011.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick does not play the games his company sells, Fortune reported, as GTA VI launches with an estimated $1B to $1.5B budget. Take-Two has not confirmed the cost, but the game has tied Metacritic’s record score and pre-orders beat expectations.

Strauss Zelnick has run Take-Two Interactive, which owns GTA studio Rockstar, since 2011. He does not play the games it sells, Fortune reported in a profile republished on Wednesday, the eve of Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch.

“I don’t think being consumer-in-chief really helps a CEO be effective in this business,” Zelnick told Business Insider.

Analysts cited by Business Insider estimate GTA VI cost $1B to $1.5B to make. Take-Two has not confirmed a figure, and Zelnick has only said the game “was expensive”.

The bet looks set to pay off. GTA VI tied Metacritic’s all-time record with a score of 99, and Take-Two said pre-orders beat expectations. Sensor Tower data puts pre-orders at 17 million, according to Fortune.

The game costs from $80 and comes without a physical disc, as Sony plans to stop making discs for new games from 2028. Its predecessor, GTA V, has sold more than 215 million copies since 2013.

Under Zelnick, Take-Two’s shares have risen more than 1,700%, and its revenue grew roughly fivefold to $5.6B in 2025. He has also said generative AI played no part in making GTA VI, which Rockstar built by hand.

#3155. Invesco QQQ Is 14% Below Its October Record. Here's Where I Think It Will Be in 2030.

The Nasdaq-100 fund trades around 14% below its October record. Can it pass that peak by the end of 2030?

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:23PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Invesco QQQ Trust ›

The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ +0.39%) closed at a record $759.66 on Oct. 6. Since then, the exchange-traded fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100 has fallen to roughly $654 as of this writing, about 14% below the high.

It's still up about 6% in 2026, but the drop has erased most of the year's gains.

Even so, I think QQQ will end 2030 at roughly $890 per share. That would put it about 17% above the October record and about 36% above today's price -- a rise of close to 8% a year, before the fund's small dividend.

That would also be a slower pace than the fund's recent run. The Nasdaq-100 itself climbed around 12% a year in the five years through October, according to Siblis Research. And my number rests on one assumption more than any other: how fast the index's companies keep growing their profits.

Showing how much profit growth has powered the Nasdaq-100, the index's total earnings climbed around 50% in the last year, according to Siblis, which removes big accounting gains. That was up from about 28% a year in the past three years and about 19% a year in the past five. In those five years, earnings outpaced the index's price by more than 6 percentage points a year. That means the valuation dropped even while the index rose.

At the end of October, the Nasdaq-100 traded at about 33 times earnings, and QQQ has slipped roughly 5% since then. By my math, this leaves the fund near 31 times earnings now.

That's a bit under where the index finished 2024 and 2025 (about 32 times earnings both years). But it's well above the 24 or so times earnings it hit at the end of 2022.

The fund isn't cheap. Still, its price-to-earnings ratio is arguably more reasonable than its recent gains would suggest, because earnings have carried most of them.

I started with the earnings. Going by the end-of-October numbers, every QQQ share represents about $21 of its holdings' earnings in the last year.

I'm assuming these earnings rise about 12% a year through the end of 2030, well below the five-year rate and a fraction of the past year's. That still puts them about 60% higher, near $34 a share.

The other piece is what investors will pay for these earnings at the end of 2030. I'm assuming 26 times earnings, about what big U.S. companies as a group sell for today. It's also under the Nasdaq-100's average of about 29 times earnings at its past 10 year-ends.

In other words, my estimate assumes the Nasdaq-100 winds up valued about like the broader market is now, with its normal premium gone. At 26 times earnings of about $34 per share, QQQ would trade at about $890 a share. Its dividend, which yields about 0.5%, could add a bit on top.

The earnings growth rate worries me more. I've already set the final valuation multiple under the index's recent average, but part of the past year's profit surge came from companies whose earnings can swing hard.

Micron Technology (MU -1.00%), one of the fund's 10 biggest holdings, is the clearest example. The memory chipmaker's revenue more than tripled to around $133 billion in its fiscal year that ended Sept. 3.

Its net income was around $85 billion, almost 10 times its net income a year earlier. But Micron's own annual report says that in the past five fiscal years, yearly changes in the average selling prices of its memory chips ranged from a rise of about 200% to a drop of about 50%.

Profits that climb so fast can fall quickly if the supply of memory chips catches up to demand, as Micron itself warns.

At 8% growth, though, the fund's earnings would reach only about $29 a share by 2030. Even at 26 times earnings, it would trade near $760. That price would just bring QQQ back to its October record after four more years.

All told, I expect QQQ to finish 2030 around $890, over its October peak but at a slower pace than investors have gotten used to. The forecast doesn't need this year's profit surge to repeat. It just needs the Nasdaq-100's earnings to keep growing at a double-digit rate once the memory chip boom cools.

Compared with the last five years, that's a modest outlook. But I think roughly 8% a year from a fund trading 14% below its record would still be a decent return.

#3154. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

#3152. AirPods Pro 3 keep getting better, here’s what’s new in iOS 27

AirPods got a variety of new features this fall in iOS 27, several of which are exclusive to AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179). Here’s everything new.

Custom EQ is a feature that some AirPods users thought Apple would never ship, but iOS 27 adds it.

With Custom EQ, Apple now lets you set your own sound profile for AirPods. Per Apple:

AirPods are designed and engineered by Apple to faithfully represent music, TV shows and movies, and calls. If you prefer a different sound profile, you can customize how AirPods represent any audio played.

You can change the EQ by going to your AirPods’ settings ⇾ Audio & Routing ⇾ Equalizer ⇾ Custom. From here, you can adjust the sound profile for low, mid, and high frequencies.

Custom EQ is available on AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Max 2, AirPods 5, and AirPods 4.

Apple GymKit has been available for years, but only for Apple Watch. It lets you pair and sync workout data with compatible cardio equipment, like treadmills, ellipticals, indoor bikes, and more.

In iOS 27, GymKit expands to support iPhone using AirPods Pro 3’s heart rate sensor. My colleague Zac gave it a try:

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

For more details on iOS 27’s GymKit feature for AirPods Pro 3, check out Zac’s full hands-on below.

Read more: iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

For most AirPods users, the single biggest upgrade in iOS 27 is Siri AI.

Siri AI is available on compatible iPhone hardware in iOS 27, and Apple made sure to expand full support for the AI assistant to AirPods too.

AirPods are essentially becoming an AI wearable thanks to the new Siri. It will let users do a lot more than the current Siri. Here are some key features via Apple’s website:

Earlier this year when AirTag 2 launched, Apple brought Precision Finding support to Apple Watch for the first time. Until now though, it’s been limited to AirTag 2.

But with iOS 27 and watchOS 27, Apple expands Precision Finding on the Watch to AirPods Pro 3.

AirPods Pro 3’s case includes the latest second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip, letting you find it with greater precision and step-by-step guidance right from your wrist.

With every batch of new AirPods features that debuts, the AirPods settings screen in the Settings app gets more cluttered.

But in iOS 27, Apple has a welcome fix: it’s redesigned and reorganized all AirPods settings.

Now, you’ll find AirPods settings organized into more categories and submenus, accompanied by colorful icons. It makes finding the right setting way easier and more intuitive than before.

Read more: iOS 27 revamps AirPods settings in a big way, here’s the new design

By Robert Izquierdo – Nov 18, 2026 at 5:24PM EST

Opendoor Technologies (OPEN +7.63%), a digital home buying and selling platform, closed at $1.27, up 7.63%. Shares rose as gains extended for a second straight session, and investors weighed housing conditions and a new deal with FSBO.com, one of the country's oldest real estate platforms dedicated to for-sale-by-owner listings.

Moreover, on Monday, Nov. 16, a deal between FSBO.com and Opendoor was announced, boosting Wall Street's hopes for a turnaround and contributing to this week's share price gains.

Also on Monday, company director Dana Hamilton bought 200,000 Opendoor shares, according to a SEC filing reported the next day. The purchase adds a governance signal, but the market still needs operational improvement to sustain this week's stock price move.

As rates go up, this hurts Opendoor's capital-intensive home-buying model, which depends on cheap debt, fast home turnover, and healthy housing demand.
