#3068. Which Laptops Last the Longest? Check Out the Laptops I’ve Tested With the Best Battery Life

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

As part of our video series Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, I share laptop recommendations and explain why battery life surged in 2026.

I can almost guarantee that your next laptop will run longer on battery power than whatever you’re currently using. We’ve seen a huge leap in laptop battery life in recent years, to the point where getting 20 or more hours on a single charge isn’t uncommon. This year alone, the average battery life of the laptops we’ve tested at CNET has increased by more than five hours. And it’s nearly doubled since the start of the decade.

With many of today’s laptops, you can leave the charger at home for days at a time. The longest-lasting laptop I tested this year lasted more than 34 hours!

This increase in battery life is one of the biggest stories in laptops this year. In the laptop episode of our video series Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, I explain what’s behind this surge in battery life and highlight some of the laptops that lasted the longest in testing.

Plus, my colleagues Kyle Kucharski from ZDNET and Joe Osborne from PCMag share their own holiday laptop picks. Kyle looks at Apple’s entry-level MacBook Neo and its imitators, and Joe breaks down what to look for in a budget gaming laptop.

Unlike raw performance, where the more you spend, the more you get, lengthy battery life can be found just as easily in a budget laptop as in an expensive, high-end powerhouse. And, in fact, less powerful components and lower screen resolutions can give cheaper laptops an edge in battery life.

The biggest factor behind longer battery life in laptops is the advancement in mobile processors. They’ve become much more power efficient, and in the case of Apple’s and Qualcomm’s chips, they’re based on an architecture other than the traditional x86 instruction set that’s been at the heart of Intel processors since the dawn of the PC era.

Apple’s run of battery-life winners started when it shifted from Intel processors to its own M-series chips. Apple’s M-series processors are based on the Arm architecture, a power-efficient chip architecture found in phones and tablets. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X-series processors are also Arm-based, and they can be found in the two longest-running laptops we’ve tested: the HP OmniBook 3 16 and OmniBook 5 14. The OmniBook 3 16’s record-setting battery performance earned it a CNET Lab Award for longest battery life.

Intel has made huge strides in processor efficiency with its last two generations of chips: the Core Ultra 200 series developed under the name Lunar Lake, and the Core Ultra 300 series, also known as Panther Lake. Last year, the Lenovo Yoga 9i 2-in-1 Aura Edition became the first Intel laptop to last longer than a day, running for 25 hours, 45 minutes in testing. It’s still the longest-running Intel laptop we’ve tested, but the MSI Prestige 14 Flip AI Plus with Intel’s next-gen Core Ultra X7 358H processor came close with a time of 25 hours, 18 minutes.

Read more: Laptops With the Best Battery Life

Whether Arm or x86, there are two more reasons behind greater processor efficiency and longer laptop battery life. For one, the size of a processor shrinks with every generation. The smaller a processor is and the more tightly packed its components are, the less power is required to flip its tinier transistors on and off. For another, today’s mobile processors feature more flexible designs with a mix of performance and efficiency cores. A processor engages its higher-performance cores only when needed, using the efficiency cores for as many general, everyday tasks as possible, so your laptop stays cool and quiet and runs longer.

For more, you can read my Labs exclusive on the huge increase in laptop battery life this year and check out the video above for my holiday laptop picks and those from my colleagues.

#3067. Goodbye, Gemini Gems: How to use Google’s new Skills – and share them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Google is retiring Gemini Gems. Here's what to do to access the same tools as Skills.

Google is replacing Gemini Gems with Skills starting Nov. 17, 2026, and it’s carrying over features that let you share Skills and add files from Google products.

Google has announced that it’s turning Gems, a Gemini feature that lets you create customizable AI chatbots, into Skills, which let you create custom instructions for Gemini. Any Gems you have created will automatically convert, but you can transfer them manually if you want to start using them now.

To help with the transition, Google revealed that two Gems features are moving, too: the ability to share creations and to include Drive, Notebook, and Photos files as part of your Skill’s instructions.

While the Gemini Gems feature is technically going away, any Gems you’ve created aren’t.

If you access the Gems portion of Gemini (since the feature is on the way out, you now have to access this through Settings), you’ll see a message that says “Starting November 17, 2026, we’ll automatically begin migrating all of your Gems to Skills.” (The cutoff date for accessing your Gems will be Dec. 16, 2026. Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit accounts will get cut off in March 2027, and Workspace education accounts will be cut off in June 2027.)

A Gemini Skill functions much the same as a Gem. You describe specific situations when Gemini should use the Skill automatically and tell Gemini what you want the Skill to do (it’s best to give specific examples of output). Google gives the example of a marketing team sharing a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines doc in Drive, or a team lead sharing an onboarding skill based on the team handbook.

The biggest difference is that Gems were standalone chats, while Skills are custom instructions that work in any conversation.

You can create as many Skills as you want, but only 100 can be active at a time.

To get users familiar with Skills, Google is bringing over two features from Gems.

First, you can now share any Skill with other users. When you share a Skill, you can choose whether the other person has permission to edit or view only. To share a Skill, go to the three-bar menu in the top left > Customize > Skills. You can view or change permissions from that screen.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

When a Skill is added, Gemini can use it automatically, or you can @mention it in chat to trigger it. One small caveat, though: you can only share Skills through the Gemini web app at the moment, not the mobile app.

Additionally, when you’re creating a Gemini Skill, you can choose to include files of up to 100MB from other Google products like Drive, Photos, and Notebook, along with files from your local device. Gemini will reference these files every time the Skill runs and update in real time, Google says. These features existed with Gems; Google is just moving them to Skills to make the new feature more comparable.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I'm an unapologetic Swag Golf fan. I love the limited drops of cool headcovers and golf apparel. Honestly, I'm a sucker for anything ultra-limited. I'm also quick to jump on anything cool that comes in a blind box or bag. The surprise sucks me in every time (and I love great golf gifts in general).

So when I found out one of the best golfers in the world, Bryson DeChambeau (he's also arguably the most famous thanks in part to his massive YouTube channel and its Break 50 series), was partnering with Swag to bring limited mystery headcovers to Dick's Sporting Goods and Golf Galaxy, I was excited.

When I got the chance to talk to DeChambeau himself about the headcovers, I had to find out where the inspiration came from. It turns out we really do "have so much time and so little to do."

If you're a fan of Bryson DeChambeau and enjoy a bit of mystery, this is a cool item to snag. Each of the 13 designs features Break 50 logos and fan-chosen designs. Four people also get to meet Bryson, go behind the scenes of a Break 50 episode, hit the range and have lunch with DeChambeau. And even if you don't win, 50 headcovers have his autograph, which gives you something else to chase.

Okay, so officially Willy Wonka has nothing to do with this project, but according to Bryson DeChambeau, "we wanted to give fans an opportunity to experience and feel something different." A blind box isn't new, though. There are lots of products in the golf space (and pop culture in general) that come in blind boxes.

But this one is a little different: "Being a Willy Wonka fan growing up, we thought there could be something cool with a golden ticket. And that golden ticket turned into a golden headcover with four different tiers."

The highest tier isn't just an incredibly limited headcover, though. The people who are lucky enough to find one at Dick's or Golf Galaxy actually get to hang out with Bryson. "They're gonna be going behind the scenes with a Break 50. They're going to have lunch with me, and I'm gonna take them to the driving range. We're gonna have a great day."

Of course, there are other prizes (besides the 13 cool headcovers). There are 50 signed headcovers in the mix, plus there are different tiers of headcovers. Tier 2 features two limited designs that are hard to come by, tier 3 has slightly more common designs, and tier 4 has the most common.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

One of the main issues with Swag is that their prices are high, with some headcovers going for more than $100 because they're limited. But this blind bag sells for $59, which is quite reasonable for a high-end headcover. "It's not at a crazy price point, DeChambeau noted. "Eventually, we want to do more stuff at even lower price points," to "grow the game of golf and grow the fan base."

But if you win, don't expect to hit a shot over Bryson's house during filming. "Insurance would probably not be happy about that," Bryson chuckled when I brought up the idea. It looks like his windows will stay safe... for now.

While Nvidia and Anthropic are under the spotlight, OpenAI and Microsoft dropped several new models this week.

It has been a wild week for AI, and it’s only Wednesday. Aside from outages, cheating scandals and upcoming IPOs, there are several new models available now. Microsoft dropped seven new versions of its MAI models at its Ignite conference, and OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, the next step forward for its flagship models.

First, Microsoft: At its Ignite developer conference on Tuesday, Microsoft introduced seven new AI models. They include MAI Cyber 2 Flash, MAI Code 2, MAI Image 2.7 and Dragon Copilot Transcribe — models meant to help with tasks in cybersecurity, coding, image generation and transcription.

It’s clear from Microsoft’s marketing that it is aiming to position its new tech as a cheaper alternative to OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s leading models, with many of these significantly cheaper to run at the enterprise level. That, plus its new licensed weight program, which lets companies customize the new AI models for their purposes, highlights how Microsoft is continuing to pitch its AI tech to the workplace.

While these new models might be useful for AI power users, they are far from most of the AI industry’s mind this week. During Tuesday’s earnings call, new interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress tried to assure investors that everything was “business as usual” after weeks of turmoil inside the company rocked the global economy. Nvidia cofounder and now-former CEO Jensen Huang’s multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, threw the company into chaos and have attracted the attention of the Securities and Exchange Commission and both chambers of Congress, where Huang has agreed to testify.

And let’s not forget about Anthropic, the Claude maker plans to become a public company this week, with the possible biggest-ever IPO slated for Thursday. Anthropic’s reportedly seeking an opening price of $78 per share, for a total valuation of $1.4 trillion — narrowly beating the other largest-ever IPO earlier this year, Elon’s Musk mega-conglomerate, SpaceX (including now SpaceXSI, because President Trump said so).

The Nvidia scandal caused a drastic 14% dip in its stock price during its first week and wiped out $1 trillion in the company’s value, but Anthropic investors don’t seem to be worried. At least, not publicly.

If nothing else, Anthropic’s IPO and the new models from OpenAI and Microsoft are stark reminders that the tech industry is nowhere near ready to slow down on AI. Even as financial, environmental and legal concerns mount — and arguably hit a fever pitch during the midterm elections — Big Tech is plowing ahead with generative AI.

#3062. Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft announced two new AI models at Ignite 2026 that promise impressive performance for much lower cost. They could reshape its relationship with OpenAI and Anthropic for good.

At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model shows 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Microsoft says MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

This doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

It’s also important to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the company paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As users adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous

There’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

This becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a company is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these new models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first

A company with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the new models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open issue.

The company also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these new models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

#3061. Apple among the companies facing pressure from US senators over ‘nudify’ apps [U: Apple responds]

The Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable users to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow users to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed users to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of New Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

Update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for users. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The company added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the company said does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

As for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

Apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The company said that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

#3060. Giving the iPhone Duo a Spin at the Apple Store? Be Sure to Test These Things Out

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Want to test out the iPhone Duo? Here are six things you need to try with it.

Now that the iPhone Duo is in stores, there are plenty of people who are curious about Apple’s first folding device. Foldables are hardly a new sector in the smartphone world, with Samsung leading the charge, but Apple’s entry into the market is a big deal, and the iPhone Duo is a stunner.

If you’re planning on checking out the iPhone Duo at the Apple store, it might be easy to just marvel at how cool it looks, but if you’re considering making this your new phone that’ll be in your pocket all of the time, you’ll probably want to get an idea of how it will be living with this new design. After all, you should be in love with all aspects of the device if you’re going to drop $2,000-plus on it.

Below, we’ve listed a handful of features and things to try out when you’re test-driving the Apple iPhone Duo in the store.

When the Duo was first revealed, Apple showed off a very intriguing animation when you unfold it. Leave it to Apple to make a function so simple look so aesthetically pleasing.

It’ll likely be the first thing you notice when you first open the Duo up to see its inner display, and there’s a good chance you’ll continue to open and close the device to see the effect. At the end of the day, it’s a parlor trick — but a very good one, adding delight to ordinary use.

Read more: The iPhone Duo Crossed 517,000 Folds and Counting in Our Custom Machine

Foldables, well, fold, and they typically come with creases. The Duo has a minimal crease and a matte display, both of which are wins. That said, even the most noticeable creases tend to “disappear” when you’re viewing content — you just get used to them while watching TV shows or YouTube videos. The Duo’s minimal crease should be even easier to ignore.

And let’s not forget about the matte screen. Several foldables ship with glossy displays, but the iPhone Duo will have a less shiny screen, making it easier to view in bright environments without annoying reflections.

The outer passport-size display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for watching videos because of how it crops content to fit the new aspect ratio. Still, it’s handy to prop the phone up in tent mode and watch shows that way. You also have a large inner display to work with, but because of its passport-style design, even that screen has a different aspect ratio than the widescreen format people are used to on regular phones, so there will likely be some letterboxing in videos.

Try watching something with the phone set up in both ways to see if it bothers you enough to dissuade you from buying the phone.

Again, it’s not an iPhone Duo issue but a foldable phone issue — the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the same size and format. The aspect ratio of the display might crop the top or sides of videos, so it’s worth trying out if you expect to watch a lot of full-screen videos.

Like videos, apps on foldables can sometimes appear a little weird, and that could be the case with the iPhone Duo‘s aspect ratio. When you’re at the Apple Store, check out how your most-used apps look and feel on both the inner and outer displays, and make sure you rotate the inner screen to see how apps behave in this orientation, too — that wide screen could be great for watching vertical videos or scrolling through social media.

If some apps, such as Instagram, look a little different or are wonky, it’ll hopefully be just a matter of time until the developers make an update that optimizes the experience for this new design. Keep in mind that you can also have two apps open onscreen at once, making it easier to multitask.

If you want the best camera experience on an iPhone right now, you should be looking at the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, but that doesn’t make the Duo a slouch for shooting photos, either.

Yes, the Duo is missing a third camera (telephoto), and if that’s important to you, then you probably shouldn’t even be considering Apple’s foldable. But still, if you’re going to shell out this much money for a new phone, test out those cameras — even if it’s in a controlled environment like an Apple Store.

Another thing to check out before you pull the trigger is your selfie shots with this new phone. There are two main ways to do this: with the phone closed, holding it up in the regular way you’d take a selfie using the outer screen’s 12-megapixel front-facing camera, or with the inner display open and shooting with the twin 48-megapixel rear cameras (the outer screen will show a preview of the shot).

There’s also a front-facing camera underneath the inner display, which is mostly for video calls — and which we suspect would produce the least-impressive shots from the device. Try them all and see what you think of the pics. And since you’re at an Apple Store, make sure you delete them afterward.

The odd but interesting aspect ratio of the front display on the iPhone Duo may be a little awkward for typing, so it’s best to do a typing test when you have one in front of you. While the inner display will provide a roomier and more comfortable typing experience, you probably won’t want to have to open up the Duo every time you want to shoot off a quick text to someone. If you have bigger hands, typing on the front screen could be a bit of a nightmare.

Typing one-handed on the small cover screen should be manageable, but try it out to see if it works for you. Some may find it convenient; others may find it cumbersome.

And when you’re typing on the inner display, try the Duo in both portrait and landscape orientations to see which feels better. You can also choose between a split keyboard and larger keys. It’s thoughtful of Apple to offer options that let you tailor the typing experience to your preferences, but you may find that none of them suit your style.

#3058. Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft could reshape enterprise spending, but there's a critical difference between estimated value and money saved.

We all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

Then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s new

What comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically says, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”

In other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving company labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026

I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

Microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the company’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the company’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:

This means the company doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

After thousands of readers were hit by last week's Outlook outage, here is how to tell an everyday technical failure from a real cyberattack

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When 52,846 readers told us in our poll that they were hit by the Outlook outage, it was a reminder of just how disruptive a single breakdown can be. Anytime an essential service stalls like that, speculation about hackers or a coordinated cyberattack quickly spreads.

The truth is far less dramatic. Almost every widespread outage often comes down to ordinary human error or fragile infrastructure rather than malicious hacking.

If your bank app freezes or your flight gets delayed by a system breakdown, here is how to figure out what is actually going on.

Digital services rely on millions of lines of code and overlapping networks, which means things break constantly.

Most major outages are caused by mundane technical failures and human error, a botched software update, a mistyped setting, a severed underground fiber cable, or a simple power failure. Unless concrete evidence of hacking emerges, an accidental technical error is almost always the safest bet.

In fact, according to the Uptime Institute, human error directly or indirectly contributes to between two-thirds and four-fifths of all data center downtime incidents — and roughly 85 percent of those human-error outages stem from staff failing to follow procedures or flaws in the procedures themselves.

When one major service goes down, it often creates a domino effect that makes other apps look broken too.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

A payment failure at a single large bank can stall transfers at several others, and a single cloud provider outage can knock dozens of unrelated websites offline at once.

Rather than trusting panicked posts on social media, check an independent outage tracker like Downdetector to see if other users are reporting problems nationwide, or search for the company’s official status page and verified newsroom account.

Major tech platforms, banks, and airlines maintain live dashboards that explain whether their systems are actually offline or just waiting on another partner to come back up.

The timeline of an outage is often one of the biggest clues to its cause.

When an engineer pushes a bad update or a server overloads, companies can usually undo the change, reroute traffic, and restore service within a few minutes or hours — though widespread system crashes can occasionally take longer to untangle.

Deep-seated cyberattacks, such as ransomware breaches, take much longer to resolve because companies have to lock down their networks, investigate the intrusion, kick intruders out, and rebuild damaged systems from scratch, a process that regularly drags on for days or even weeks.

In the first few hours of a major breakdown, nobody, not even the company experiencing the crash, always knows the exact root cause.

When hackers are behind a major disruption, they often claim credit publicly to demand ransom or score political points, or federal cybersecurity officials eventually confirm a breach after investigating.

Until an affected company or government agency shares verified findings, patience is the best defense against bad rumors.

#3054. Here's What a $1,000 Investment in Kraken Robotics Will Be Worth by the End of 2027 if Undersea Drone Orders Keep Doubling

Down 70% from its high, would a doubling of drone revenue in 2027 be enough to drive a big rebound for Kraken Robotics stock?

By Keith Noonan – Nov 18, 2026 at 7:15PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Kraken Robotics ›

Following strong gains in 2025 and an impressive run-up through the first three months of this year, the tide has turned for Kraken Robotics (KRKNF -3.67%) stock. The company's share price has been hit with strong bearish pressure, and it now trades down 40% over the last year and 70% from the lifetime high that it reached in March.

The company specializes in subsea and maritime technologies, and the batteries and sensor systems it sells for underwater drones are central to its stock story -- but the market appears to have become far less optimistic about how much these products can drive growth. With that in mind, what would it mean for $1,000 invested in Kraken stock at today's prices if undersea drone orders double in 2027?

Before diving more specifically into what a doubling of Kraken's underwater drone component sales in 2027 would mean for the company's stock, it's worth detailing some of the factors that have caused the company's share price to pull back so sharply.

There are several catalysts at play here, and understanding the dynamics will help model the business's growth opportunities in the category in relation to moves for its stock.

In addition to these catalysts, Kraken continues to rely heavily on stock-based compensation to fund its operations. This allows the company to operate without burning through cash, but the creation of new stock dilutes shareholders' positions.

Kraken's subsea drone business focuses on selling batteries and sensors to companies rather than building completed drones itself. In addition to this business, the company also sells towed synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) systems, other subsea sensors, and software. Its business is also significantly more diversified following the acquisition of Covelya. Still, the subsea drone market appears to be Kraken's most important near-term growth driver.

So, what would a doubling of the company's subsea drone revenue in 2027 mean for its valuation? It might not be enough to spur gains in the stock because many investors are banking on even higher growth.

While Kraken is attracting interest from other players in the drone space, Anduril is currently its most important customer by a wide margin. Anduril is the next-gen defense tech company responsible for the Dive-LD and Dive-XL subsea drones and the Ghost Shark drones built with Australia on the Dive-XL platform.

Anduril is working to ramp up production of these drones in 2027, and that could cause Kraken's drone business to more than double if it retains its component wins. For example, Anduril expects that production of Dive-LD drones will increase from roughly 50 this year to its full production rate of roughly 200 by the end of next year. Production for the Dive-XL drones, which are larger and use more batteries, should also see big scaling next year.

So what would a doubling of the company's drone market mean for a $1,000 investment in Kraken stock? Assuming other important dynamics that affect its share price remain relatively constant, I think a doubling of drone-related revenue could mean the stock trades in roughly the same range as now. There may be moderate upside, depending on how the market reacts to the lifting of uncertainty. Big sell-offs this year already seem to bake in softer growth, and a doubling of drone revenue next year would seemingly reflect a ramp that's slower than previously anticipated.

#3052. Zane Lowe shares Apple Music Radio audience numbers, recalls ‘crickets’ in the early days

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue said Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:

We were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a big way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:

The really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very important to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a new logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe said he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:

We could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The issue of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a company and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift…

#3051. Nvidia’s Earnings Calmed Markets, but AI’s Harsh Reckoning Marches On

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Jensen Huang's departure was only a symptom of a bigger problem in the AI economy.

Though Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday offered some reassurance to investors after Jensen Huang’s departure as CEO, it did little to resolve the political, regulatory and leadership questions hanging over the entire AI economy.

The semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI infrastructure boom saw its shares plunge by 35% from last month’s high following the scandal around Huang — wiping out nearly $2 trillion in market cap and triggering Wall Street panic around a broader AI reckoning.

Nvidia’s finance chief and interim CEO, Colette Kress, sought to project stability, telling investors it was “business as usual” and raising Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 outlook. Though the chipmaker’s stock price rebounded after reporting better-than-expected results, it’s likely to face a rocky future, as concerns linger around national security violations amid illegal export deals. Market confidence is also shaky amid supply chain backlogs for advanced chips and servers that remain critical to AI compute and the training of large language models.

In the lead-up to the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Huang issued a statement that he would return as CEO if the board of directors decides it’s in the “best interest” of shareholders and the country. Despite calls from President Donald Trump and other tech executives to reinstate the former GPU boss, Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia’s appointed first-ever chair of the board, said there is no intention to reinstate Huang, and no successor was named.

Prior to the call, The Wall Street Journal reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Huang over concerns that the company misled investors.

Huang maneuvered Nvidia into a linchpin role for frontier AI labs and data center firms, not just by supplying hardware but also by providing equity, credit and financial backing and by mobilizing third-party capital to secure investment for the AI buildout of data centers. Nvidia’s circular financing schemes — in which the chipmaker helps fund a hyperscaler like Meta or Microsoft, which then uses the funds to buy its products — were allegedly a source of contention for Kress and other executives.

Critics have warned that this kind of vendor financing inflated the AI bubble by inflating growth projections and buoying the market valuations of chipmakers and hyperscalers.

According to Reuters, Kress was expected to pull back from some of the riskiest AI financial deals, including investments in OpenAI and AI infrastructure companies such as Lambda. Already, Nvidia has significantly scaled back financing for a $250 billion OpenAI data center deal. During Tuesday’s call, Kress failed to announce a sweeping unwind of Huang-era financing arrangements, focusing more on continuity than retreat.

Kress mentioned that chip producer TSMC, a key Nvidia partner, will continue working with Nvidia despite Huang’s departure. The company also said it was assuming no China data-center compute revenue in its next fourth-quarter outlook.

Nvidia supplies the lion’s share of the hardware necessary for data center construction and model training, and the company has long said that the demand for chips exceeds supply. Shortages of RAM and high-bandwidth memory slow down the production of AI servers and raise prices for cloud companies and other buyers. In an attempt to buy its way out of the bottleneck, Nvidia has committed large sums of money to secure future memory supply.

If Nvidia distances itself too much from its GPU commitments, that could be a problem for the entire tech industry. Semiconductor production is an incredibly specialized field dominated by very few companies, and any changes to the supply chain could have ripple effects on global markets and vendors, including in consumer electronics and cloud services.

Huang’s affair with a Chinese executive connected to the Singapore-based Megaspeed — whom US intelligence claimed was a Chinese intelligence asset — complicated an already tight supply chain. Megaspeed was under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms obtain high-value Nvidia chips through channels that violated US export controls.

According to the investment research firm Culper, up to one-fifth of Nvidia’s fiscal-year 2026 compute revenues were driven by movement of some of the company’s most advanced chips into China through nonrestricted intermediary countries in a process called diversion. When advanced Nvidia chips or servers are illegally routed to Chinese buyers, those units are no longer available to legal customers in the US and allied markets.

Huang was influential in shaping the Trump administration’s chip export policies, pushing back against export controls that limited Nvidia’s sales to China. But the recent scandal prompted new Commerce Department restrictions on chip shipments through third countries.

While Kress cited improving supply and sustained demand in raising Nvidia’s outlook, stricter export rules and tighter controls could further constrain capacity by creating more obstacles to compliance and delivery.

Nvidia’s better-than-expected earnings may steady investors in the short term, but any company that supplies essential hardware for the AI buildout is at risk if investor confidence in the industry falters. When Nvidia reports strong growth, AI-focused stocks and funds with large technology holdings are likely to go up. When Nvidia’s outlook weakens, investors worry that AI spending is slowing or that companies have overcommitted.

A handful of big tech companies — colloquially known as the Magnificent Seven — make up a big share of major funds and indices. Five of them account for roughly 30% of the S&P 500 index, and AI overexposure in those businesses translates into overexposure in many individual retirement accounts and 401(k)s. Because index funds hold substantial positions in Nvidia and other large tech companies, an AI selloff could affect retirement balances even for people who don’t own Nvidia shares directly.

The Magnificent Seven are heavily affected by AI stock swings. Alphabet’s stock price sank as Nvidia news aftershocks reverberated through the markets, proving that top firms are not unassailable. Other tech companies heavily focused on AI infrastructure, such as Intel and CoreWeave, likewise saw their share prices decline.

Despite growing concerns about AI dangers, Huang was one of AI’s most aggressive promoters, framing the technology as an economic and national security imperative. In early September, the now-disgraced CEO said that artificial general intelligence, or AGI, had arrived, congratulating OpenAI on its GPT-6 Astra model, which was trained on Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell GPUs.

Huang pushed against recent warnings from AI researchers, calling for unrestrained progress on frontier models and repeatedly arguing against new laws and safety regulations.

Even before Huang’s business and personal scandals came to light, AI companies were gearing up for a post-midterm-election PR campaign, as the technology has become increasingly unpopular and the backlash against data centers has grown. Democratic Party politicians pushed a platform to shift the federal government’s lax approach toward the AI industry. Some Democrats are also poised to craft legislation to prevent an AI industry bailout in the event of a bubble pop.

Amid bipartisan calls for Huang to testify before Congress, many politicians are also seeking to investigate high-ranking members of US intelligence and the Commerce Department for allowing export loopholes or for failing to act on knowledge of Nvidia’s China-related deals.

Kress might be able to lead Nvidia with tact and diligence, separating the company from some of its riskiest deals. But the national security implications of her predecessor’s relationships have opened up a can of worms that no CEO can close on their own.

The federal government is ruled by inertia, but right now there’s some investigative momentum aimed directly at the major AI players. That will almost certainly ice out some investor hype. It’s clear the AI industry is facing a reckoning that was not in the cards just months ago.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5

MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

“You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, said during the keynote.

The approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft said it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman said of the new coding model the company announced at Ignite.

The company also released its new image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic, PBC ›

With Anthropic (ANT +0.00%) set to roll out its initial public offering (IPO) on Thursday, not everyone will be able to get in on the expected initial list price of $83. To get that, you had to be a large entity or have access to a brokerage that received some allocation of shares that were priced at the initial price. When a stock goes public, it rarely starts trading at its initial list price due to high demand.

So, if you missed out on the allocation, you'll have to purchase shares on the open market, likely at a higher price than the initial list price.

Will this be worth doing? Let's take a look.

Some stocks execute their IPO without a lot of fanfare. Others get plenty of attention and tend to see their stock skyrocket by the end of the first day of trading. The majority of IPOs follow a common trend: They rise during the first week, then sell off.

Something similar happened with Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.27%) earlier this year in what was then the largest IPO in history based on funds raised (Anthropic is projected to surpass it). When measured by valuation, SpaceX is likely to retain the “largest” title. Anthropic was projected to go public at a $2 trillion valuation earlier this year and set a new record, but that won't happen now due to lower interest in AI investments compared to earlier this year.

The lower valuation forecast could end up being a reason why Anthropic doesn't follow the typical initial rise-and-fall pattern, as interest in AI investing has already taken a bite out of Anthropic's initial estimated price tag.

If you want to invest in Anthropic on Day 1, you’ll have to buy shares on the open market, which could mean paying an inflated price compared to what those who got in at the IPO price paid. Still, if Anthropic continues its tremendous growth pace (its revenue increased 12 times year over year to $17 billion in Q3), that price tag could be worth it in a few years.

If you do buy Anthropic shares, just remember that you should be buying for the long term, not to take advantage of a one- or two-day gain. You should be buying the stock to own the company, not to rent it short-term. Anthropic has real potential to be a fantastic business that is rapidly growing and pioneering the AI-first world. It also has risks associated with it that need to be factored in. It has a huge runway, and with the world just scratching the surface of what's possible with AI, now could be a great opportunity to own a winner.

Just because you missed out on the initial allocation of Anthropic stock doesn't mean you have to miss out completely on the IPO.

Based on the bestselling 2009 romance novel by British author David Nicholls, "One Day" charts the slow-burn romance between University of Edinburgh grads Emma Morley and Dexter Mayhew — played by the winning duo of Ambika Mod and Leo Woodall, who share a wonderfully natural, palpable chemistry — over the course of two decades, catching up with the characters on the same date every year.

#3042. Fathom Forthcoming: First Battery Cells Roll Out of Ford’s Michigan Plant for Electric Pickup

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Ford's BlueOval Battery Park Michigan is shipping its first lithium iron phosphate cells to Louisville for Fathom prototypes, a key milestone for the automaker's next-generation EV.

This week, Ford began shipments of the first lithium iron phosphate electric vehicle battery cells from its new BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall, Michigan, to its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. There, the prismatic cells will power early Ford Fathom electric pickup truck prototypes and validation vehicles. The automaker invited me into the plant to meet the people who build the batteries and to see how the so-called “jelly roll” is made.

In 2025, consumers lost access to the clean vehicle tax rebates of the Inflation Reduction Act, but the program and its incentives remain in the law for automakers and suppliers. So bringing this US-based, domestically owned battery plant online is kind of a big deal for Ford. It’s an important milestone for the automaker’s plan to make its new Universal Electric Vehicle, or UEV, platform a reality and to bring the Fathom — its upcoming electric pickup truck — to market in 2027 at a price that EV-eager customers can stomach.

Ford expects to sell the upcoming Fathom at an estimated price of $28,350 (well, $29,945, including the $1,595 destination and delivery fee), with the first preorder expected to open early next year.

BlueOval Battery Park Michigan is a $3 billion, 2 million-square-foot facility with a targeted annual production capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours. That’s a whole lot of batteries. Ford is expected to employ 1,700 people at the site across two 12-hour shifts, running around the clock to reach that capacity.

The plant is a clean facility, so getting in meant donning a clean suit, mask, hairnet, gloves and two layers of shoe booties. I then crossed special magnetic and sticky floor panels designed to pull any metal particles off the bottoms of those booties, before passing through multiple air-blower airlocks that blasted my body clean of loose dust.

From the outside, the building is huge and difficult to take in completely. On the inside, the scale truly comes into focus as I stare down a massive hallway just under a mile long end to end. Raw materials — rolls of copper and aluminum sheet, plus the chemical powders that coat them — enter the plant at the eastern end, move in a straight line through the facility, and completed battery packs exit at the western end. The first 0.7 mile of the fab belongs to cell production, split between isolated cathode and anode lines that join halfway through for final cell assembly.

Ford engineers, battery experts and executives tell me that the automaker chose lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, chemistry in a prismatic (rectangular) format for its affordability and structural benefits. LFP uses no nickel or cobalt, which keeps costs down, and Ford found the chemistry well suited to bidirectional charging.

To keep costs low enough to deliver a reasonably priced car, Ford couldn’t use a Chinese supplier and still qualify for IRA manufacturing credits. So it licensed the technology from one, working with a company called CATL, which one Ford exec described as “the world’s leading battery manufacturer,” whose batteries power 30 million vehicles worldwide.

Despite working with a Chinese company, Ford says the plant is completely US-owned, staffed and operated and is totally IRA-compliant, with no foreign entity of concern, or FEOC, involvement beyond the licensing agreement.

Charles Poon, who leads vehicle hardware engineering, said Ford didn’t simply copy a catalog part.

“We designed a unique cell that does not exist in the CATL catalog, specifically for the UEV,” Poon said, adding that the taller and simpler cell delivers “the energy density, the affordability, the durability that [Ford is] looking for” and allows the automaker to more completely integrate the cells and battery pack into the vehicle’s design.

Ford also had to build the supply chain, Poon said, sourcing an IRA-compliant stream for a battery chemistry that is only just entering the mainstream in North America, and working with approved global partners and North American suppliers.

On the cathode and anode assembly lines, meter-wide rolls of copper and aluminum are first coated with a chemical slurry that is baked on. The large rolls are then split into 10 smaller rolls, with tabs notched into their exposed edges at set intervals. As the continuous rolls pass through multiple machines like gigantic cassette players, AI-powered vision systems watch the foil for coating defects, scratches and wrinkles, marking problem sections so they can be automatically removed.

Next, the cathode and anode foils are layered and rolled into a cylinder, then pressed flat into what Ford calls a jelly roll. Imagine a roll of toilet paper mashed in a hydraulic press, and you’ll have a good idea of what it looks like: a flat rectangle with rounded ends.

The jelly rolls are then gathered in pairs, and the previously exposed tabs are folded together and ultrasonically welded to more solid terminals, which are in turn laser-welded to a cap. The jelly roll couple is then laser-sealed into an aluminum box, about the size and weight of a masonry brick, to form a nearly complete prismatic cell. Engineers vacuum out the air, check for leaks by pressurizing the cell with helium, and fill it with liquid electrolyte. Bob’s your uncle: you have a finished LFP prismatic cell.

Ford says the assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, which plant manager Tracy Church says makes BlueOval Battery Park “among the fastest LFP prismatic lines outside China.”

From the cell line, completed prismatic cells would normally pass through a door and straight into pack manufacturing, where full battery packs with integrated “e-box” electronics, integrated cooling and wiring are built. That part of the plant is still undergoing validation, so for now Ford is shipping just the cells to Louisville, not complete battery packs. The company plans to have pack manufacturing up and running in Marshall ahead of Fathom’s launch, with full pack deliveries to Louisville planned in 2027. Church told me that the plant aims to produce 50 battery packs per hour.

Ford hasn’t officially specified the energy capacity of the cells or the completed battery packs and wouldn’t comment when asked about expected range for the Fathom. The automaker wouldn’t even confirm how many cells go into the EV’s pack, but I estimate between 90 and 108 cells based on a cutaway of the finalized unit I examined (but wasn’t permitted to photograph) during my tour. I expect Ford is holding off on finalizing details until closer to the EV’s 2027 launch window.

Battery Park Michigan isn’t just sending cells to Kentucky; it’s also sending expertise. Ford’s Glendale Kentucky plant — which used to build batteries for the F-150 Lightning full-size electric pickup — is currently being retooled to build LFP cells for Ford Energy for large-scale energy storage applications, and the lessons Ford learns in Michigan are already being shared with the manufacturing teams there.

Ford has been in the EV business for over 15 years. In 2011, it revealed the Focus Electric at CES. 2019 brought the debut of the Mustang Mach-E — which Ford recently found is holding up well after years on the road with minimal battery degradation — followed by the arrival of the F-150 Lightning in 2021. #3037. Not Safe, Not Creative: 123456 Is Still the World’s Most Common Password

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

Data breaches, hacks and cyberattacks. Guess what? Our passwords are still risky.

Our data keeps getting hacked, breached, stolen and exposed, and yet we’re still using the most predictable passwords.

For the seventh time in the past eight years, 123456 is the world’s most common password, and it’s got other uncreative companions on the list, according to the latest analysis by password and passkey manager NordPass, a division of Nord Security. The top three most used passwords in the US were: 123456, password and admin. Yikes.

In the 44 countries analyzed, the password 123456 was used more than 7.2 million times. The rest of the top 10 passwords: admin, 12345678, 123456789, 1234, 12345, password, Aa123456, Pass@123 and 1234567890.

NordPass said that even though many people prefer simple, easy-to-remember passwords, much more awareness of password safety is needed. The company recommends creating a unique password for each account that’s at least 15 characters long, including uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and special characters. Though it’s tempting to reuse the same passwords, hackers rely on that complacency.

NordPass suggests upgrading weak, old passwords to stronger ones. You can also add multifactor authentication, which requires an additional layer of security beyond a login password. That could mean entering a one-time passcode sent by text or email, answering security questions, or using facial recognition or fingerprint ID.

CNET managing editor Adam Benjamin said that the risk isn’t primarily from someone randomly guessing your password. The danger is from algorithms that collect data or bots that use credential stuffing (in other words, stolen username and password pairs obtained from a data breach).

According to Benjamin, using an obscure reference or a different language doesn’t make a password stronger. “A password is good when it’s too much trouble for an algorithm to crack,” he said.

You might remember the scene from the 1987 movie Spaceballs, where the combination to Planet Druidia’s air shield is 12345. Dark Helmet calls it “the stupidest combination I’ve ever heard in my life!” and says it’s “the kind of thing an idiot would have on his luggage.” The joke remains a staple reference for weak passwords and PINs, and yet, here we are.

Last year, two researchers hacked into McDonald’s hiring chatbot by guessing the password 123456 to access 64 million data records, including applicant names, email addresses and phone numbers.

In 2023, the Akira ransomware group hacked into KNP Logistics Group, a 158‑year‑old UK transportation firm, by guessing an employee’s weak password. The hackers locked the company’s data and demanded a $6.6 million ransom, forcing KNP to shut down and lay off 700 workers.

This year, suspected Iranian hackers gained access to US water supply systems due to internet-connected devices that used default passwords — or none at all.

The rise of the AI era has also made password hacking easier. One study even found that some AI systems could determine people’s passwords by listening to their keystrokes.

NordPass has conducted its Top 200 Most Common Passwords analysis since 2019. To compile its lists, NordPass and independent researchers examined passwords exposed in public data breaches and dark web repositories, then organized and categorized the data by country of origin.

NordPass has found that password habits are heavily influenced by current trends and culture. Over the last several years, some of the top three passwords have been Lebron0319 (in reference to NBA star LeBron James), Savage20 (musical group) and roblox.com1 (video game). In the 2010s, the top three were Lachimolala (meme), telegram (social media) and minecraft (video game).

But while these passwords might make us feel nostalgic for these time capsules of experiences, interests and entertainment, they don’t translate to strong internet security. “Unfortunately, fandoms make for terrible passwords,” the NordPass report notes.

Passwords based on pop culture, current events and sports can be easily predicted or cracked in seconds using automated tools, especially if your interests are visible on public social media profiles. Adding a number to the end of a password doesn’t help — attackers program their tools to test common number combinations and symbol swaps.

Given all the accounts we deal with — financial institutions, social media, stores, government agencies — creating dozens of unique passwords and remembering them can be exhausting and annoying.

“Inventing passwords that meet that criterion across hundreds of logins is virtually impossible, which is why we recommend password managers to create long, complex passwords and then store them all for you,” said Benjamin.

A password manager creates and updates passwords for apps, Wi-Fi networks and websites, ensuring that all your passwords are unique and resistant to bot attacks. Another plus is that you don’t have to remember them or write them down: They’re stored in an encrypted vault you can access by verifying your identity. Password managers can also auto-fill login credentials.

CNET senior writer Joe Supan said the best password managers also offer passkeys, which are ways of logging into apps and websites using biometric ID, such as facial or fingerprint scans, or PIN codes. “These are really the sign-in methods of the future, and I probably wouldn’t recommend a password manager that doesn’t include them at this point,” Supan said.

CNET’s top two recommendations for password managers are NordPass and Bitwarden.

Property owners pay wholesale rates and charge tenants below retail, and a 12-month lease rollover builds the recurring base over time.

10 stocks we like better than Elauwit Connection ›

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 16, 2026, Elauwit (ELWT +0.01%) announced that monthly recurring revenue, or predictable subscription income, reached $539,000 at quarter-end. That growth matters to long-term investors because recurring subscription revenue creates high-margin cash flow after initial network setup. Three things management said stand out.

Elauwit signs five-to-eight-year contracts with property owners to provide managed Wi-Fi networks across entire apartment communities. Once installation finishes, resident leases roll over onto the network over about 12 months, creating a steady stream of recurring subscription fees.

Property owners purchase internet at wholesale rates and charge tenants a technology fee below typical retail prices. The resulting spread increases net operating income (NOI), the property profit before debt and taxes, which raises total property market value.

As Elauwit expands its footprint across 31 states and Washington D.C., concentration in key cities enables hiring local employees instead of third-party contractors. That shift cuts operational expenses while accelerating technical response times for property managers.

Real estate investment trusts (REITs), entities that own income-producing property, are adopting managed Wi-Fi quickly, and Elauwit is winning portfolio deals through its land-and-expand strategy. Management is building local market density to lower service costs and support margins.

Contracted networks become long-lived recurring revenue once activated. Building owner relationships remain central to expanding recurring revenue.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order.

Twenty percent of holiday shoppers are using AI agents as their first stop for research and advice, but they are not ready to have agents make purchases, according to the latest Salesforce research.

Also: What to know about early Black Friday sales

Salesforce surveyed more than 2,500 shoppers in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia and found that 74% of shoppers trust recommendations from AI agents. Salesforce research forecasts AI-driven shopping recommendations to drive $75.8 billion in Cyber Week spending, up 13% from 2025.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer

Brands are also being noticed by AI agents, with 30% of shoppers saying they were first introduced to a new brand via AI. And most importantly, 1 in 10 (11%) shoppers would avoid a brand if an AI agent told them to.

Here are some of the key findings from the 2026 holiday shopping research.

Retailers that use AI shopping agents are seeing bigger orders and more loyal customers. The survey found that shoppers who use AI agent referrals are twice as likely to make a purchase. In addition, 39% of shoppers have used AI agents on an e-commerce site, and 80% had a positive experience, while 75% felt more loyal to the brand as a result of the AI agent experience.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order. Brands that use AI agents are seeing seven times faster sales growth than brands without them.

1 in 3 consumers has used an AI agent, including the widely adopted Meta Muse, now used by 12% of all consumers. Grok Bot is also in high demand.

The survey found that 28% of consumers give their agents multiple tasks per day. The most common use of AI agents is price comparisons, product reviews, and brainstorming for gift items. Brand discovery is a major benefit of AI agent use cases.

Agents as advisors are growing, but agents are not buying products yet, with only 19% of personal agent users using logic to check out. Only 9% of consumers allow their personal AI agents to have unrestricted access to their financial details, and 36% have set up a separate credit card for their AI agents.

Also: ZDNET’s favorite tech devices for 2026

The majority of consumers (73%) are not comfortable giving personal AI agents their payment information, and 49% are not interested in agents making purchases on their behalf. Consumers do not want to share their purchase history or personal data that could potentially lead to unwanted charges. Shoppers will abandon an AI agent after 2-3 mistakes. If an AI agent makes a bad recommendation, 1 in 3 consumers will blame the AI.

Retailers must adopt AI shopping agents in order to compete. Retailers must be able to service and respond to shopper agents. The ability to detect intent, buying signals, sources of dissatisfaction, and other consumer-related buying patterns at machine scale (significantly faster and higher volume than human scale) will require retailers to invest in AI agentic engagement capabilities.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Today, AI agents advise consumers on their holiday shopping journeys, but in the very near future, they will autonomously make purchasing decisions with little to no involvement from their human counterparts. The future of shopping will be more autonomous, highly personalized, and nearly frictionless. Brands that invest in agentic AI will garner the most loyalty and future business.
